result: The PBMC-NSG humanized mouse model successfully recapitulates HIV-1 infection in GALT, with productive infection demonstrated by blood p24 levels and presence of infected cells in colon crypts at 21 days post-infection, consistent with previous BLT mouse studies.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 collectively demonstrate successful HIV-1 infection in PBMC-NSG mice with blood p24 measurements (C17), immunofluorescence showing infected cells in colon (C18), electron tomography confirmation (C19), and consistency with prior BLT model results (C20). The convergent evidence from multiple imaging modalities and quantitative viral load data strongly supports model validation.

result: Tissue clearing techniques (CLARITY/PACT and CUBIC) combined with immunofluorescence successfully visualized human T-cells and HIV-1 p24 in lymphoid tissues from humanized mice, revealing both infected T-cells and p24 signal not associated with T-cells.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 describe the successful application of tissue clearing methods to visualize immune cells and virus in intact tissues. The methods are well-established (C22-C23), and the imaging results (C24-C26) demonstrate technical feasibility. However, the interpretation of p24+/CD3- signal (C26) as either free virions or non-T-cell infection is inferential and requires EM validation.

result: Longitudinal quantification of GALT infectivity revealed peak infection at 10-12 days post-infection (nearly 3% of cells), preceding peak blood viral load by 9 days, followed by rapid decline in infected T-cells and progressive CD4+ T-cell depletion.
evaluation: Claims C27-C35 present a comprehensive longitudinal analysis with automated quantification validated at 96.2% accuracy (C28). The temporal disconnect between tissue infectivity (peak at 12 days, C32, C34) and blood viral load (peak at 21 days, C34-C35) is well-documented with quantitative data. T-cell densities in uninfected mice (6%, C29) are reasonably comparable to human samples (10-12%, C30), though the difference could be significant.

result: Spatial analysis of HIV-1 infection in colon revealed preferential localization of CD4+ T-cells and infected cells to intestinal crypts and lower villi, while CD8+ T-cells distributed uniformly, with this spatial pattern remaining constant despite progressive depletion of CD4+ T-cells and infected cells over time.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 provide detailed spatial quantification showing statistically significant differences in cell localization (C40: CD4+ at 51.2±34.5 μm vs CD8+ at 79.2±36.8 μm, p<0.0001). The findings are consistent with prior studies in BLT mice (C41) and SIV-infected macaques (C42). The inference that depletion is due to target cell loss (C45) is reasonable but not directly proven.

result: Electron microscopy revealed temporal dynamics of HIV-1 in GALT: minimal detection at 5 days post-infection, exponential increase with large extracellular virus pools and ~10% of crypts showing active infection at peak (10-16 days), followed by reduced infected cells and virus pools at later times (>21 days), with most late-stage virus pools not associated with actively infected cells.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 describe EM observations across infection time course. The progression from undetectable (C46) to peak infection with >100 virions in pools (C47-C48) to decline (C49-C50) is well-documented. The inference that p24+/CD3- signal represents free virions rather than infected non-T-cells (C51) is supported by convergent IF and EM data, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

result: Electron tomography revealed virus pools in lamina propria near vasculature with 3D tracing showing virus-containing intercellular spaces opening to blood vessel walls, suggesting a route for systemic viral dissemination.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 describe ET visualization of anatomical connections between virus pools and vasculature. The 3D reconstruction provides strong structural evidence for potential routes of viral spread, though functional confirmation of viral entry into circulation would require additional experiments.

result: PBMC-NSG mice exhibit altered splenic architecture compared to wildtype mice, with white pulp present as smaller striations rather than circular foci, but retain essential structural and cellular components including HIV-1 target cells, collagen, and distinct red/white pulp regions.
evaluation: Claims C60-C68 systematically compare spleen architecture across mouse strains using brightfield microscopy, IF, and EM. The characterization demonstrates that while PBMC-NSG spleens differ from wildtype (C67), they contain necessary components for HIV-1 studies (C68). The inference that the model is suitable despite architectural differences is reasonable but assumes altered architecture doesn't affect infection dynamics.

result: Electron tomography of HIV-1-infected spleen at 12 days post-infection revealed prolific virus production with individual cells producing thousands of virions: one cell contained nearly 1000 particles in a 19.3 μm³ volume (846 mature, 18 immature, 102 budding), extrapolating to >6000 virions per cell per replication round; another cell showed 1350 particles in 13.9 μm³, predicting >4000 virions released.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74 present quantitative ET data with precise virion counts from reconstructed volumes. The extrapolation to total cellular production (C73: >6000 virions) relies on approximating cell volume as an ellipsoid, which introduces uncertainty but is a reasonable geometric approximation. The calculations are internally consistent between two independent cells (C72, C74).

result: Discrete electron densities at the base of budding virions were identified by electron tomography and confirmed by immuno-EM to contain VPS4, suggesting these densities include VPS4 possibly in complex with other proteins involved in viral budding machinery.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79 combine ET structural observations with immuno-EM validation. The localization of anti-VPS4 antibodies to the same region as the densities (C78) provides strong evidence for VPS4 presence. The inference that densities may include VPS4 in complex with other proteins (C79) is appropriately cautious given the resolution limits of the techniques.

result: Cells undergoing prolific virus budding (>100 budding profiles) exhibited large cytoplasmic accumulations of electron-dense structures (hundreds to thousands) within 1 μm of the plasma membrane, distinct from ribosomes and absent in cells with minimal budding, suggesting these densities accumulate during active virus production and are depleted after virus release.
evaluation: Claims C80-C87 describe a novel observation of cytoplasmic densities correlated with prolific budding. The exclusion of ribosomes based on morphology (C83) is well-reasoned. The correlation between density presence and active budding (C84-C86) is compelling, though the sample size appears limited. The inference about accumulation/depletion dynamics (C87) is logical but represents a snapshot interpretation rather than direct temporal tracking.

result: There is a temporal disconnect between tissue infectivity and blood viral load, with tissue infection peaking before blood viremia.
evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by the longitudinal data showing peak tissue infection at 12 days PI when blood p24 is low, with blood p24 peaking at 21 days PI when tissue infection is declining. This is corroborated by citations to human studies showing similar patterns.

result: At 21 days post-infection, there was increased p24 signal not associated with CD3+ T-cells concurrent with decreased T-cell infectivity.
evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by quantitative IF data and is consistent with EM observations showing virus pools not associated with actively infected cells at later timepoints. This suggests accumulation of free virus or infected non-T-cells.

result: Comparison with SIV studies and the observed high viral production in tissues suggests HIV-1-infected cells undergo multiple rounds of virus release and that tissue-based virus production contributes significantly to blood viral load and systemic spread.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 involve extrapolation from SIV data (C102: 4.0-5.4×10⁴ virions) to HIV-1 and inference about multiple release rounds (C103) and contribution to systemic spread (C104). While the reasoning is logical and supported by the observation of thousands of virions per cell, direct evidence for multiple rounds of release from the same cell and quantitative contribution to blood viral load is not provided.

result: The parallel multiscale imaging approach combining 3D-IF of optically cleared tissue and electron tomography enabled visualization of early HIV-1 spread at both single-cell and subcellular resolution, allowing longitudinal spatial assessment of T-cells and virus proteins in intact tissues and detection of individual virions and subcellular complexes.
evaluation: Claims C105-C107 accurately summarize the methodological achievements of the study. The combination of tissue clearing with IF for cellular-level analysis and ET for subcellular detail is well-demonstrated throughout the results. This represents a technical advance in HIV-1 tissue imaging.

result: HIV-1 represents a major global health challenge with the majority of target cells residing in tissues rather than blood, particularly in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, lymph nodes, and spleen, which serve as key sites for virus replication and disease progression.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 establish the epidemiological and biological context for the study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature (UNAIDS 2015, Guy-Grand and Vassalli 1993, Kilby 2001, Haase 1999, etc.). These represent well-accepted background knowledge.

result: Humanized mouse models, particularly PBMC-NSG mice, provide a suitable system for studying HIV-1 infection as they reconstitute human immune cells including activated T-cells (the primary HIV-1 target), recapitulate key aspects of HIV-1 pathology, and exhibit infection kinetics with peak blood viremia at 2-4 weeks post-infection.
evaluation: Claims C6-C16 justify the use of humanized mouse models with extensive citations to prior literature. The characterization of PBMC-NSG mice (C8-C9, C14-C15) and comparison with BLT mice (C16) is well-supported. The biological rationale focusing on activated T-cells (C10-C13) is sound.

result: The PBMC-NSG model predominantly harbors activated human T-cells that may cause graft-versus-host disease, and the lack of other cell lineages combined with elevated T-cell activation may enhance HIV spread dynamics compared to other humanized mouse models, though the model has been successfully used for therapeutic studies.
evaluation: Claims C96-C98 acknowledge important limitations of the PBMC-NSG model. The characterization of the model's features (C96) and potential effects on infection dynamics (C97) are appropriately cautious. Prior use for therapeutic studies (C98) is well-cited. This represents appropriate discussion of model limitations.

result: The study employs established techniques including optical clearing for large-volume tissue imaging, electron microscopy and tomography for ultrastructural analysis, and builds on prior knowledge of spleen anatomy and HIV-1/SIV pathology in lymphoid organs.
evaluation: Claims C21, C54-C59, C75, C99-C101 describe established methodologies and anatomical/biological knowledge that provide context for the study. All are appropriately cited to prior literature. These represent standard background information and methodological justification.

result: The imaging methods developed in this study are proposed to be adaptable to other animal models and human patient samples, with potential future applications for visualizing biological processes during early HIV-1 spread and developing quantifiable spatial maps of tissue infection.
evaluation: Claims C94, C108-C110 represent speculative statements about future applications and adaptability of the methods. While the techniques are likely transferable, no data is provided demonstrating application to other models or human samples. These are reasonable projections but remain unvalidated hypotheses.

result: Summary of key findings: peak gut infection at 10-12 days post-infection when blood viral loads were low, with infected cells localized to crypts and lower villi; minimal detection at 5 days progressing to ~10% of crypts infected by 10-12 days; and thousands of virions released by individual cells in spleen with cytoplasmic densities near sites of prolific virus production.
evaluation: Claims C88-C93 summarize the main experimental findings of the study. These are well-supported by the detailed data presented in other claim groups and represent accurate synthesis of the results. This is appropriate for abstract/summary content.

result: During heterosexual HIV-1 transmission, the virus crosses the genital epithelium, infects target cells, establishes latent reservoirs, expands locally, and spreads systemically via lymph and blood.
evaluation: Claim C95 describes the established model of HIV-1 transmission and dissemination, supported by citation to Fackler et al., 2014. This represents accepted background knowledge about HIV-1 pathogenesis.
